steps.body: Plans differ in value. If profit is P = 2x + y, every feasible point has a score — and we want the highest. Here's the gift: on a straight-fenced region, the maximum of a linear objective always lands ON A CORNER. So don't search the infinite interior; interview the two or three corners.

explanationVariants: P = 2x + y at (6, 0) is 12 — beating (0, 0)'s 0 and (0, 6)'s 6.
The corner scores are 0, 12, 6; the all-muffin corner wins with 12.

widget.prompt: Feasible triangle corners: (0, 0), (6, 0), (0, 6). For P = 2x + y, what is the LARGEST corner score?

commonErrors.feedback: That's (0, 6)'s score. (6, 0) earns 2·6 + 0 = 12 — muffins pay double.
That would need (6, 6) — infeasible. The best corner is (6, 0) at 12.
The origin scores 0 — the worst corner, not the best.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Score every corner: P(0,0) = 0, P(6,0) = 12, P(0,6) = 6. The best is 12 — and it sits at a corner, not inside.

widget.prompt: Slide P: the line 2x + y = P sweeps across the plane. Estimate the LARGEST P whose line still touches the feasible triangle.
widget.lowFeedback: The line still cuts through the region — richer plans remain. Push P higher.
widget.highFeedback: The line has left the triangle entirely — no feasible plan earns that much.
widget.successFeedback: P = 12: the sweeping line's last touch is exactly the corner (6, 0). That's WHY corners win — a straight line leaving a straight-sided region exits through a vertex.

predict.prompt: As P grows, the line 2x + y = P slides without tilting. Its LAST contact with the region will be…
predict.reveal: A straight line sliding across a polygon exits through a vertex (or, in ties, a whole edge ending in vertices). Either way a corner attains the maximum — that's the corner principle, seen rather than memorized.

steps.body: So the algorithm is short: find the corners (boundary pairs), score each with the objective, keep the best. Different objectives crown different corners — P = x + 3y on the same triangle pays (0, 6) eighteen, dethroning (6, 0). The region sets the menu; the objective picks the meal.

explanationVariants: P = x + 3y scores the corners 0, 6, 18 — the all-scone corner (0, 6) now wins.
Tripling y's pay moves the crown: 0 + 3·6 = 18 beats 6 + 0 = 6.

widget.prompt: Same corners (0, 0), (6, 0), (0, 6), new objective P = x + 3y. What is the best score now?

commonErrors.feedback: That was the OLD objective's champion. With y paying 3, (0, 6) earns 18.
That's (6, 0)'s new score — muffins only pay 1 apiece now.
24 would need (6, 6): infeasible then, infeasible still.

widget.fallbackFeedback: New objective, same corners: P(0,0) = 0, P(6,0) = 6, P(0,6) = 18. Changing the objective can move the winner to a different corner.

explanationVariants: The minimum also lands on a corner: cost C = x + y is smallest at (0, 0), scoring 0.
Corner scores 0, 6, 6 — the cheapest plan is the origin, doing nothing.

widget.prompt: For COST C = x + y on the same triangle, what is the smallest corner score?

commonErrors.feedback: Both loaded corners cost 6, but (0, 0) costs nothing — minima ride corners too.
12 was the MAXIMUM of the profit objective — under cost C = x + y the corners score 0, 6, and 6, and the minimum is 0.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Cost wants the SMALLEST score: C(0,0) = 0 beats every other corner. Minimizing and maximizing both happen at corners.

explanationVariants: P = x + y scores (6, 0) and (0, 6) equally at 6 — the objective line is parallel to the cap edge, so the WHOLE edge is optimal, corners included.
Both cap-line corners score 6; every point between them does too, since x + y = 6 along that edge.
hints: Score all three corners under P = x + y.
(6, 0) → 6 and (0, 6) → 6. What does x + y equal along the whole line between them?
The edge IS x + y = 6: the objective is constant along it.

widget.prompt: Under P = x + y, corners (6, 0) and (0, 6) tie at 6. Which feasible plans achieve the maximum?

options.label: Every point on the edge x + y = 6
options.feedback: The objective runs parallel to that boundary, so the entire edge maxes out — with its corners still among the winners.

options.label: Only the two corners
options.feedback: The midpoint (3, 3) also scores 3 + 3 = 6 — the whole edge ties.

options.label: The centroid of the triangle
options.feedback: Interior points satisfy x + y < 6 — strictly poorer than the edge.

takeaways: Linear objectives peak (and bottom out) at vertices.
Algorithm: find corners → score → keep the best.
Ties spread along an edge, but a corner always shares the crown.
